Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
- What the test expects:
  The test aiffFilesAreNoTARs opens an AIFF audio file and passes it to ArchiveStreamFactory.createArchiveInputStream(InputStream). Since an AIFF is not an archive, the factory should throw an ArchiveException with a message starting with “No Archiver found…”.

- How the factory detects formats:
  ArchiveStreamFactory.createArchiveInputStream reads small signature prefixes to detect ZIP/JAR/AR/CPIO (12 bytes) and DUMP (32 bytes). For TAR it reads the first 512-byte block and first tries TarArchiveInputStream.matches(header, len). If that returns false, it applies a relaxed fallback:
  - If at least 512 bytes are available, it wraps those 512 bytes in a ByteArrayInputStream, constructs a TarArchiveInputStream over it, and calls getNextEntry() to “verify the header checksum”.
  - If getNextEntry() doesn’t throw, the factory assumes it is a TAR and returns new TarArchiveInputStream(in). Any exception during this probe is ignored and detection continues.

- Why the AIFF file is misidentified as TAR:
  - The AIFF file’s first 512 bytes do not contain the TAR magic/version strings, so TarArchiveInputStream.matches(...) correctly returns false.
  - The relaxed fallback then tries to parse those 512 bytes as a TAR header by creating a TarArchiveInputStream over them and calling getNextEntry().
  - Because the fallback only checks that getNextEntry() doesn’t throw (and swallows exceptions), certain non-TAR payloads can slip through if TarArchiveEntry construction and checksum validation don’t fail hard for that specific byte pattern. In this case, the AIFF file’s header happens to pass the permissive parsing path, so no exception is thrown during getNextEntry().
  - As a result, ArchiveStreamFactory concludes the stream is a TAR archive and returns a TarArchiveInputStream instead of throwing an ArchiveException.

- How this causes the test failure:
  The test expects an ArchiveException with message “No Archiver found…” when passing an AIFF file. Due to the overly relaxed TAR detection (the COMPRESS-117 fallback), ArchiveStreamFactory returns a TAR stream instead, so the test reaches fail("created an input stream for a non-archive") and fails.

- Root cause:
  The “relaxed” TAR detection heuristic in ArchiveStreamFactory is too permissive: it treats any input as TAR if a speculative parse of the first 512 bytes via TarArchiveInputStream.getNextEntry() doesn’t throw, even when the TAR magic/version don’t match. This can incorrectly classify non-archive files (like AIFF) as TAR archives.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
